effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative primary empirical case study; descriptive administrative/budget figures and cooperative general assembly vote counts (14 to 4) are reported, with no statistical effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Outside urbanized zones in the Canton of Lucerne, citizens must self-organize water provision via cooperatives supported by federal and cantonal agricultural subsidies (up to 30% each). New Public Management (WOV/NPM) reforms outsourced cantonal technical planning to private engineering firms (140–160 USD/hour out of a 1.5 million USD annual cantonal budget), inflating planning costs, limiting user co-design, and pushing scheme mergers and professionalization. In the studied interconnection project of three cooperatives (S, K, and N), cantonal officials withheld federal subsidies and warned of indeterminate payment delays for independent refurbishment to compel Cooperative N to join a shared reservoir; Cooperative N successfully blocked full organizational merger in favour of an umbrella reservoir cooperative while voting 14 to 4 at its general assembly to continue planning the connection.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised with CASP Qualitative Checklist (design ceiling = 2). Rated 2 because the lead author directly observed the administrative, subsidy, regulatory, and planning mechanisms operating on rural water schemes from inside both the cantonal agency (LAWA) and the commissioned engineering consultancy, corroborated by 17 semi-structured interviews and archival records.

mechanism_flags.comment: Spatial planning law restricts municipal water duty to urbanized zones, leaving rural households outside built-up zones self-responsible via common-property cooperatives with agricultural-only subsidy eligibility (ELIGIBILITY: zoning, service_area, property). Two-step municipal/cantonal subsidy applications, outsourced commercial engineering rates, water tariff/pumping cost concerns, and threatened subsidy payment delays create administrative/financial burdens (BURDEN: planning, fees, procedural_steps, delay). Cantonal officials exercise broad subsidy discretion and outsourced technical support while cooperatives negotiate governance and user participation across municipal/cantonal/cooperative tiers (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, bureaucratic_assistance, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination). The food security department issued a compliance ultimatum over reservoir standards, and cooperative leaders weighed but declined court appeal due to cost and time (ENFORCEMENT: sanction, judicial_review).

evidence_quotes.quote: In response many independent, collective water schemes emerged in rural areas. We describe these schemes as commons, since citizens organize legal, institutional, and infrastructural aspects of water access in a collective manner.

These insights were enriched by in-depth, semi structured interviews with six government officials (four current and two former), five scheme officials, three engineers, two local politicians and one contractor. In addition, the historical and the newspaper archive of the Canton was consulted.

Since the Canton has a fixed annual budget to support drinking water infrastructure for farming households (1.5 million USD), there is a constant spending pressure to initialise and plan new projects.
